distinguishing_feature: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by restriction of energy intake without engaging in recurrent binge eating or purging behaviors.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with characteristic features of anorexia nervosa but lacks specific subtype documentation regarding binge-eating/purging or severity level.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with profound, debilitating fatigue and post-exertional malaise rather than core psychopathology centered on body weight, distorted self-image, and intentional weight loss.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of recurrent binge eating and purging behaviors rather than strict caloric restriction alone.
[LLM DRAFT] Higher body mass index (BMI) corresponding to the mild severity threshold rather than the extremely low BMI seen in extreme severity.

[LLM DRAFT] Presents with generalized weakness that may stem from diverse neuromuscular, metabolic, or systemic conditions rather than primary weight-related caloric deprivation and body image distortion.
[LLM DRAFT] Persistent dangerously low body weight and ongoing severe restriction rather than weight restoration and symptom remission.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of recurrent binge eating or purging behaviors rather than purely restricting behaviors.
[LLM DRAFT] Diagnostic criteria lack sufficient detail to specifically categorize as restricting type or confirm current remission status.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging behaviors.
[LLM DRAFT] Significantly lower body mass index corresponding to severe or extreme clinical severity thresholds.
[LLM DRAFT] Lack of core psychological features such as intense fear of gaining weight or distorted body image.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of recurrent binge eating and purging behaviors rather than solely restricting intake.
[LLM DRAFT] Lower body mass index (BMI) reflecting a more severe degree of emaciation and physiological compromise.
[LLM DRAFT] Absence of core eating disorder criteria for a sustained period following a previous diagnosis.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging behaviors such as self-induced vomiting or misuse of laxatives.
[LLM DRAFT] Body mass index falls below the extreme severity threshold of 15 kg/m² alongside more profound physical and metabolic compromise.
[LLM DRAFT] Higher body mass index meeting the mild severity threshold with less pronounced physiological impairment.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging behaviors such as self-induced vomiting or misuse of laxatives.
[LLM DRAFT] Body mass index (BMI) falls below the extreme severity threshold defined by DSM-5 criteria (typically BMI < 15 kg/m²).

[LLM DRAFT] Presentation of characteristic anorexia nervosa symptoms where specific subtyping (restricting vs. binge-eating/purging) or severity cannot be definitively determined due to insufficient clinical information.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by prominent caloric restriction and weight loss without binge eating or purging behaviors, with severity specified.
[LLM DRAFT] Accompanied by recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging behaviors rather than restriction alone.
[LLM DRAFT] Demonstrates a previous history of anorexia nervosa with criteria no longer met for a sustained period.

[LLM DRAFT] Presents with acute intravascular volume depletion due to hemorrhage or fluid shifts across all pediatric age groups, whereas neonatal dehydration is primarily characterized by hypernatremia or total body water loss often related to feeding difficulties.
[LLM DRAFT] Neuroimaging reveals acute parenchymal blood rather than an ischemic infarct.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of thunderclap headache and xanthochromia or blood in the basal cisterns on imaging.
[LLM DRAFT] Causative etiology is a distinct vascular pathology such as cerebral venous sinus thrombosis or vascular malformation rather than thromboembolic infarction.
[LLM DRAFT] History of ischemic rather than hemorrhagic cerebrovascular event on neuroimaging
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of sudden thunderclap headache and meningeal signs rather than focal intraparenchymal hematoma symptoms
[LLM DRAFT] Bleeding located in subdural or extradural spaces rather than primarily intracerebral tissue
[LLM DRAFT] History of ischemic stroke rather than subarachnoid hemorrhage on neuroimaging.
[LLM DRAFT] Primary parenchymal hemorrhage on neuroimaging rather than subarachnoid blood.
[LLM DRAFT] Intracranial hemorrhage originating from an alternate non-subarachnoid source.
[LLM DRAFT] Preceded by acute ischemic stroke symptoms confirmed by neuroimaging demonstrating cerebral infarction rather than other cerebrovascular etiologies.
[LLM DRAFT] Often accompanied by a sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache and meningeal signs rather than isolated focal deficits.
[LLM DRAFT] Associated primarily with a parenchymal bleed rather than other nontraumatic intracranial hemorrhage locations (such as subdural or epidural).
[LLM DRAFT] Typically preceded by a sudden 'thunderclap' headache rather than other forms of nontraumatic intracranial hemorrhage.
[LLM DRAFT] Caused by ischemic tissue infarction rather than a primary intracranial hemorrhage.
[LLM DRAFT] Confirmed by neuroimaging demonstrating ischemic infarct rather than unspecified vascular etiology.
[LLM DRAFT] Confirmed by neuroimaging showing acute primary parenchymal bleeding.
[LLM DRAFT] Typically accompanied by sudden 'thunderclap' headache and meningeal signs rather than isolated vascular deficit.
[LLM DRAFT] Represents a follow-up visit for previously diagnosed heat fatigue rather than a new initial presentation.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by significant intravascular volume depletion and hemodynamic instability independent of ambient temperature exposure.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents specifically in neonates with inadequate fluid intake or excessive loss, unrelated to environmental heat stress.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents during or immediately after acute heat exposure rather than as a delayed or chronic sequela.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by long-term, relapsing fatigue and post-exertional malaise independent of a history of heat exposure.
[LLM DRAFT] Manifests primarily with signs of acute intravascular volume depletion such as hypotension and tachycardia, which may occur without environmental heat exposure.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents during the acute exposure episode rather than as a follow-up visit for a resolved or ongoing prior event.
[LLM DRAFT] Represents a chronic, long-term residual complication rather than a routine subsequent clinical encounter for recent heat fatigue.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by objective signs of significant intravascular volume depletion and electrolyte imbalance rather than isolated heat-induced fatigue symptoms.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with sunken fontanelles, lethargy, and inadequate wet diapers specific to neonatal physiology and feeding issues.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by self-imposed severe caloric restriction and distorted body image rather than acute fluid or blood loss.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with temporary heat-related discomfort and fatigue without the profound intravascular volume depletion or hemodynamic instability seen in hypovolemia.
[LLM DRAFT] Accompanied by gastrointestinal symptoms like constipation or diarrhea with relative bradycardia rather than prominent hemorrhagic manifestations.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by a step-ladder fever pattern, rose spots on the trunk, and hepatosplenomegaly without the mucosal bleeding typical of Lassa fever.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents predominantly with atypical pneumonia and a history of livestock exposure rather than acute viral hemorrhagic fever features.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by post-exertional malaise and profound fatigue rather than true objective neuromuscular weakness.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with persistent generalized exhaustion and lethargy following a documented viral infection, lacking primary muscle pathology.
[LLM DRAFT] Manifests with acute circulatory compromise, tachycardia, and orthostatic hypotension rather than primary neuromuscular weakness.
[LLM DRAFT] A clear temporal link to a documented non-viral infection rather than the multi-system criteria required for ME/CFS.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents as prolonged fatigue specifically following a recognized viral illness without the full constellation of ME/CFS neuroimmune and autonomic symptoms.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by a primary decrease in maximal voluntary muscle force rather than the hallmark post-exertional malaise (PEM) seen in ME/CFS.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, and cognitive impairment lasting at least six months without a confirmed preceding acute infection.
[LLM DRAFT] Follows a definitively identified viral infection rather than other types of pathogens or unspecified infectious agents.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with acute fatigue and exhaustion directly linked to environmental heat exposure rather than an antecedent infection.
[LLM DRAFT] Caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Paratyphoid B (Schottmülleri), historically associated with more prominent gastroenteritis symptoms.
[LLM DRAFT] Caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Paratyphoid C, which is rare and frequently presents with septic shock or focal suppurative infections.

[LLM DRAFT] Caused by Salmonella typhi rather than Salmonella paratyphi A, traditionally presenting with a more severe clinical course and higher rates of classic complications like intestinal perforation.
[LLM DRAFT] Clinically indistinguishable from paratyphoid B, differentiated solely by the specific causative subspecies of Salmonella (Salmonella Paratyphi A vs B).

[LLM DRAFT] Clinically very similar enteric fever syndrome, but caused specifically by Salmonella Paratyphi C and historically more commonly associated with septic complications or localized suppurative lesions.

[LLM DRAFT] Generally presents with a more insidious onset, sustained high fever, and higher rates of severe gastrointestinal complications (such as intestinal hemorrhage or perforation) compared to typical paratyphoid fevers.
[LLM DRAFT] Clinically indistinguishable presentation caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Paratyphoid A, typically diagnosed via blood or stool culture to differentiate the specific serovar.
[LLM DRAFT] Clinically similar enteric fever caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Paratyphoid B, often associated with more prominent gastrointestinal symptoms than other paratyphoid types.
[LLM DRAFT] Caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi, historically presenting with a generally more severe clinical course and higher rates of classic complications like intestinal perforation.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by multi-system symptoms lasting at least 6 months with defining post-exertional malaise, whereas postviral fatigue is often shorter-term or less strictly defined.
[LLM DRAFT] Fatigue linked to non-viral infections or generalized post-infectious states rather than specifically documented preceding viral triggers.
[LLM DRAFT] Acute onset directly tied to environmental heat exposure and dehydration rather than an antecedent viral infection.
[LLM DRAFT] Fatigue improves somewhat as the pregnancy progresses into the second trimester compared to the first.
[LLM DRAFT] Fatigue is persistent and disabling beyond standard pregnancy duration, accompanied by post-exertional malaise and unrefreshing sleep.
[LLM DRAFT] Fatigue is accompanied by severe restriction of caloric intake, intense fear of gaining weight, and body image distortion rather than normal pregnancy physiology.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of severe first-trimester nausea and vomiting (hyperemesis gravidarum) rather than the relative mid-pregnancy lull.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of hallmark post-exertional malaise and unrefreshing sleep lasting six months or longer, independent of gestation.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of core psychopathology regarding body image distortion and significantly low BMI rather than normal gestational weight gain.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with prominent hemorrhagic manifestations, pharyngitis, and sensorineural hearing loss, often linked to rodent exposure in West Africa.
[LLM DRAFT] Associated with body lice infestation and characterized by relapsing five-day fevers accompanied by severe shin pain.
[LLM DRAFT] Marked by a more insidious onset with sustained high fever, relative bradycardia, and characteristic rose spots on the trunk.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with prominent mucosal bleeding, pharyngitis with exudates, and sensorineural hearing loss, unlike the typically self-limiting febrile nature of sandfly fever.

[LLM DRAFT] Often features atypical pneumonia or granulomatous hepatitis with prominent occupational exposure to livestock, distinguishing it from the phlebotomine vector-borne presentation of sandfly fever.

[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by relapsing fever cycles lasting about 5 days associated with body lice infestation, whereas sandfly fever is transmitted by sandflies and follows a brief 3-day febrile course (three-day fever).
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with atypical pneumonia and prominent hepatic involvement rather than vector-borne relapsing fevers associated with body lice.
[LLM DRAFT] Associated with rodent-to-human transmission via excreta in endemic West African regions, often presenting with pharyngitis and mucosal bleeding.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by a sustained stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, and gastrointestinal symptoms like constipation or pea-soup diarrhea.
[LLM DRAFT] Caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Paratyphoid A, often presenting with a slightly milder clinical course than typhoid fever.
[LLM DRAFT] Caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Paratyphoid B, more frequently associated with prominent gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea.

[LLM DRAFT] Caused by Coxiella burnetii and typically features prominent atypical pneumonia or granulomatous hepatitis rather than the characteristic sustained high fever and relative bradycardia of typhoid.
